guides.title: How to read a research paper
guides.summary: A three-pass method, a map of the results, and a one-page reading sheet. Read for what the paper proves and how, not line by line from page one.
guides.body:
Most researchers read far more papers than they write. Yet few of us were ever taught how to read one. The usual mistake is to start on page one and push through every line until the end. This is slow, tiring, and it rarely leaves a clear picture of what the paper actually does.

A paper is not a novel. It is a structured argument with a few main claims and a supporting network of definitions, lemmas and references. Read it the way it was built.

## Decide why you are reading

Before opening the PDF, write one line: *why am I reading this?* The answer decides how deep you go.

- **Screening.** Is this paper relevant to my project at all? Ten minutes is enough.
- **Using a result.** I need Theorem 3.2 and its exact hypotheses. Go straight to it, then check every definition it depends on.
- **Learning a method.** I want to reuse the technique. Here you need the proofs.
- **Refereeing or reviewing.** You need everything, including what the paper does not say.

## The three-pass method

The method below is adapted from S. Keshav, *How to Read a Paper* (ACM SIGCOMM Computer Communication Review, 2007). It works in every field.

**First pass (10 minutes): the shape of the paper.** Read the title, the abstract and the introduction. Read the section titles. Read the statements of the main theorems, but not their proofs. Look at the bibliography and note the references you already know. At the end you should answer five questions: what is the problem, what is the main result, what kind of paper is it (new theory, new method, survey, computation), what does it build on, and is it well written.

**Second pass (one hour): the content.** Read the paper in order, but skip the long proofs. Read every definition, every statement and every example. Draw the figures again if they matter. Mark the references you will need. At the end you should be able to explain the main results to a colleague, with their hypotheses, without looking.

**Third pass (several hours): reconstruct the paper.** Read the proofs. Better, try to prove each statement yourself before reading the proof. When the author writes "it is easy to see", check that it is easy. This is the pass where you find the hidden assumptions, the clever trick that makes the paper work, and sometimes an error.

Most papers only deserve the first pass. A few deserve the third. Being honest about this is how you keep up with a field.

## Build a map of the results

A long paper is a graph. Each result depends on definitions and earlier results, some internal and some cited from other papers. Drawing this graph is the fastest way to understand the architecture of a paper.

1. List the main theorems (often labeled Theorem A, B, C in the introduction).
2. For each one, find the lemmas and propositions its proof uses.
3. Mark the results imported from other papers with their exact reference, for example *[12, Proposition 4.3]*.
4. Mark the one or two steps where the real difficulty lies.

The map tells you what you can safely skip, and what you must understand to use the paper. It also shows you where new work is possible: a hypothesis that is used only once, a lemma that seems stronger than needed, a special case that is never discussed.

## Keep a one-page reading sheet

For every paper that passes the second pass, write a short sheet. Keep the format fixed so that sheets are easy to compare months later.

- **Reference.** Authors, title, year, arXiv number or DOI.
- **Problem.** One or two sentences.
- **Main results.** Stated precisely, with hypotheses.
- **Method.** The key idea of the proof in a few lines.
- **Dependencies.** The results it imports, with exact references.
- **What is new.** Compared to what was known before.
- **Open questions.** Those stated by the authors, and your own.
- **Connections.** Links with your work or with other papers you know.

A reading sheet takes twenty minutes to write. It saves hours when you return to the paper, and it is the raw material of the introduction of your next article.

## Read actively

- **Work through an example.** Take the simplest non-trivial case and compute everything in it. Many results become obvious in an example, and many errors become visible.
- **Test the hypotheses.** Remove one hypothesis and look for a counterexample. If you cannot find one, either the hypothesis is not needed or you have not understood the proof.
- **Check the notation.** Write a small glossary of the symbols. Papers often change notation between sections.
- **Follow citations precisely.** When a proof cites another paper, open the exact statement. A result is often cited in a form slightly different from the one that was proved.

## When you are stuck

Getting stuck on a line is normal. Mark it, continue reading, and come back later. The answer is often three pages further, or in the next paper of the same authors. If you are still stuck, ask: a colleague, your supervisor, or the authors themselves. Researchers are usually happy to answer a polite and precise question about their work. The guide on [research methodology](research-methodology.html) explains how to write such an email.

## Summary

- Know why you read before you read.
- First pass for the shape, second for the content, third for the proofs.
- Draw the map of the results and their dependencies.
- Write a one-page reading sheet for every paper you keep.
- Read with a pencil: examples, counterexamples, exact references.

guides.title: Tools for finding, reading and managing papers
guides.summary: Where to search, how to follow new work, how to read PDFs efficiently and how to keep a library you can still use in five years.
guides.body:
Good tools do not replace reading, but they remove most of the friction around it: finding the right paper, knowing when something new appears, jumping to a cited result, and finding your own notes again a year later. Below is a working set. Most of it is free.

## Searching the literature

- **arXiv** (arxiv.org). The preprint server for mathematics, physics, computer science, statistics and more. Most recent work appears there first. Learn the listing pages of your categories and the advanced search by author, title and abstract.
- **Google Scholar** (scholar.google.com). Broad coverage across all fields. Its most useful feature is *Cited by*: it lists the later papers that cite a given paper, which is how you follow an idea forward in time.
- **zbMATH Open** (zbmath.org). A free database of reviews for mathematics, with precise subject classification (MSC codes), author profiles and links between papers. A short review is often the best first pass on an older paper.
- **MathSciNet** (subscription, usually through your library). The other major reviewing database for mathematics, with the Mathematical Citation Quotient for journals.
- **Field databases.** PubMed for life sciences, Scopus and Web of Science for citation data across fields, DBLP for computer science, INSPIRE for high-energy physics.
- **Semantic Scholar** and **Connected Papers** show graphs of related work. They are useful to find the papers you did not know to search for.

A good habit: when you find a key paper, read its bibliography *and* its list of citing papers. The first tells you where the idea comes from, the second where it went.

## Following new work

You cannot search every week by hand. Let the new papers come to you.

- **arXiv email alerts.** Subscribe to the daily listing of one or two categories. Skim titles every morning. Five minutes a day is enough to know your field.
- **Google Scholar alerts.** Create an alert for the names of the people whose work you follow, and for a few precise keywords. Also follow the *citations* of your own papers.
- **Journal tables of contents.** Most journals offer email or RSS alerts for new issues.

Keep the bar low for opening a paper and high for reading it in full. The guide [How to read a research paper](reading-a-paper.html) explains the three passes.

## Reading PDFs

A PDF reader for research should do three things well: show you a citation without losing your place, let you annotate, and keep your annotations with the file.

- **[VanoLib Reader](https://github.com/yassine-aitmohamed/vanolib-extension)** is a free, open-source PDF reader for papers that works in Chrome, Edge and Brave. Clicking a citation shows the reference immediately, with a verified link. Clicking "Figure 3" or "Table 2" shows the figure in place. It supports highlights, notes, a night mode and export of all annotations, and it can copy a reference in BibTeX, AMS, APA, MLA or Chicago style.
- Other options include the Google Scholar PDF Reader extension, which also previews citations, and Skim on macOS, which previews internal links on hover.

Whatever you use, annotate with a purpose: one color for definitions, one for main results, one for things you do not understand yet.

## Managing your library

After a few years, a researcher has read thousands of papers. Without a system, you will reread papers without remembering that you have read them already.

- **Reference managers.** Zotero (free, open source) and JabRef keep your references, PDFs and BibTeX in one place. Zotero's browser connector saves a paper with one click. Export a `.bib` file per project.
- **One BibTeX file per paper you write.** Keep entries clean: correct capitalization in braces, DOI, journal name in full, and arXiv number for preprints. Check each entry against the publisher's page, not against an automatic import.
- **Reading sheets.** Keep your one-page sheets (see the reading guide) next to the PDFs, named by first author and year, for example `Weinstein1983-local-structure.md`.

## Writing and organizing projects

- **[VanoLeaf](https://github.com/yassine-aitmohamed/VanoLeaf-LaTeX-Editor)** is a LaTeX editor in the spirit of Overleaf that runs on your own computer: file tree, source on the left, PDF on the right, click-to-jump, no account and no compile timeout. Long theses compile to the end.
- **[VanoShelf](https://github.com/yassine-aitmohamed/vanoshelf-extension)** adds order to the Overleaf projects page: sort projects into fields, hide the ones you do not want on screen, and blur titles in a shared office.
- **[VanoAtlas](https://github.com/yassine-aitmohamed/vanoatlas)** is a local research workspace that keeps projects, tasks, meetings, notes, papers and LaTeX in one private app.
- **[VanoNote](https://github.com/yassine-aitmohamed/VanoNote)** is a handwritten notebook and classroom whiteboard for pen tablets, with PDF annotation and a live link for students.

All four are free and open source (MIT license). The [Tools page](../tools.html) lists them with installation links.

## A minimal setup to start today

1. Subscribe to the arXiv listing of your main category.
2. Create Google Scholar alerts for five researchers you follow.
3. Install a reference manager and a PDF reader with citation previews.
4. Create one folder per project with its PDFs, reading sheets and `.bib` file.
5. Spend ten minutes every morning on new titles, not more.

guides.title: Writing your first paper in English
guides.summary: The anatomy of a research paper, the order in which to write it, and the sentence-level habits that make English academic prose clear, even when English is not your first language.
guides.body:
Many researchers write their first paper in a language that is not their own. This is not a weakness. Clear academic English is a small, learnable language: short sentences, precise words, and a fixed set of conventions. Elegance comes later. Clarity comes first.

## The anatomy of a paper

Every section answers one question for the reader.

| Part | The question it answers |
|---|---|
| Title | What is this paper about? |
| Abstract | What does it prove or find, in a few sentences? |
| Introduction | Why does it matter, what is new, and what are the main results? |
| Preliminaries | What does the reader need to know, and with which notation? |
| Main sections | How are the results proved or obtained? |
| Examples or applications | What do the results give in concrete cases? |
| References | What does the paper build on? |

A reader decides from the title whether to read the abstract, from the abstract whether to read the introduction, and from the introduction whether to read the rest. Most of your readers will stop somewhere along the way. Write each part so that it is useful even if the reader stops there.

## The order in which to write

Do not write the paper in reading order.

1. **The results.** Write the precise statements of the main results first, with their hypotheses. Everything else is organized around them.
2. **The proofs and the body.** Write the technical sections. Notation will change while you work. That is normal.
3. **The preliminaries.** Now you know exactly which definitions and known results the body uses. Include those, and only those.
4. **The introduction.** Now you know what the paper really does.
5. **The abstract and the title.** Last, when the content is fixed.

## Before you write: discuss the strategy

Before writing a single formal proof, write half a page that explains the strategy: what the key idea is, which known results it relies on, and where the difficulty lies. Discuss it with your supervisor or a co-author. A wrong strategy found at this stage costs an afternoon. Found after twenty pages of LaTeX, it costs weeks.

## Sentence-level habits

**Short and direct sentences.** One idea per sentence. If a sentence has three clauses, try splitting it. Semicolons are rarely needed in mathematical prose. A period is almost always better.

**Subject, verb, object.** "We prove that the map is injective" is better than "It is the injectivity of the map that is proved here."

**Use "we".** In mathematics and many sciences, "we" is standard and natural: "we prove", "we show", "we construct". Refer to your own earlier papers in the same way ("in [3], we showed"), not as "the author".

**Strong, precise verbs.** Prefer *prove, construct, classify, characterize, determine, establish, extend* to vague verbs like *study, consider, deal with, look at*.

**Define before you use.** Every object and every symbol must be defined before its first use, and defined only once. If a definition appears in the introduction, do not repeat it in Section 2. Refer back to it.

**One notation, kept fixed.** Choose your notation once and keep it in the whole paper. Use the standard notation of your field when it exists. Do not rename objects without a reason.

**Cite precisely.** Write "by [12, Theorem 4.3]", not "by a result in [12]". The reader should be able to find the exact statement in seconds.

**Do not reprove what is known.** If a result is in the literature, cite it with its exact number and use it. Do not restate it as a new Proposition and do not reprove it.

**Avoid empty phrases.** Cut "It is worth noting that", "It is well known that" (when it is not), "In this regard", "Moreover, it should be emphasized that". These add length and remove clarity.

## Small grammar points that matter

- **Articles.** "A" introduces a new object, "the" refers to one already known. "Let $G$ be a group. The group $G$ acts on…".
- **Tense.** Use the present for mathematics and for what the paper does ("We prove", "Theorem A shows"). Use the past for history ("Weinstein proved in 1983").
- **"Which" and "that".** "The map that we construct" (restrictive, no comma). "The map, which is smooth, …" (additional information, with commas).
- **Do not start a sentence with a symbol.** Write "The group $G$ is abelian", not "$G$ is abelian" at the start of a sentence.
- **Hyphens.** "A well-known result" before a noun, but "the result is well known" after the verb.

## Learning from good writing

Choose three or four papers in your field that you find very clear. Read them again, this time for the language. Copy into a notebook the phrases you like: how they announce a result, how they introduce a definition, how they begin a proof. This personal phrasebook will serve you for years.

## A checklist before sending the draft to anyone

- [ ] Each main result is stated precisely, with all its hypotheses.
- [ ] Every symbol is defined before its first use, and only once.
- [ ] Every cited result has an exact reference number.
- [ ] No known result is reproved.
- [ ] Each section begins with a sentence that states its goal.
- [ ] The notation is the same in every section.
- [ ] The abstract and the introduction match what the paper actually proves.

The next guides go deeper into [the abstract](writing-the-abstract.html), [the introduction](writing-the-introduction.html), [the presentation of results](presenting-results.html) and [revising paragraphs](revising-paragraphs.html).

guides.title: Writing the abstract
guides.summary: An abstract is a short, exact advertisement for the paper. Start with what you prove, give every main contribution, use strong verbs, and leave the symbols out.
guides.body:
The abstract is the most read part of your paper. Editors read it to choose referees. Researchers read it in the daily arXiv listing and decide in a few seconds whether to open the PDF. It must be short, exact, and it must make the contribution visible.

## Principles

**Start with the result.** The first words should say what the paper proves, constructs or determines. Do not open with "We study", "In this paper, we consider" or a sentence of general background. The reader already knows the field from the title.

**Give every main contribution.** If the paper has three main results, the abstract mentions all three, including the one announced in the title. Usually three or four sentences of content are enough.

**Use strong verbs.** *Prove, construct, classify, characterize, determine, establish, extend, introduce.* Avoid weak verbs that make a result sound routine: *compute, deduce, give, study, discuss, consider*.

**No symbols, no formulas.** Describe objects in words. "We classify the simple modules" is readable by everyone. A formula in an abstract is read by no one, and many listing services display it badly.

**Do not undersell.** Do not describe a main result as "a tool", "a technical lemma" or "a key step". Do not present your theorem as "a special case of" something else if it is not. If the result is new, say what it is.

**Do not oversell.** Every sentence of the abstract must be true and must be proved in the paper. No "for the first time" unless you have checked. No adjectives like "novel", "powerful" or "elegant". Let the result speak.

**One consistent notation and terminology.** Use the same names for the objects as in the title and in the theorems.

**Prose, not a list.** An abstract is one paragraph of continuous text. It usually has no citations.

## A structure that works

1. **Main result.** "We prove that…" or "We classify…".
2. **Second and third contributions.** "We also construct…", "As an application, we determine…".
3. **Optional: method or context in one sentence**, only if it is itself a contribution ("Our approach relies on a new … which also applies to …").

Four to six sentences, often 80 to 150 words. Check the length limit of the journal.

## Before and after

The paper below is invented and its statements are only illustrative, but the problems in the first version are common.

> **Before.** In this paper, we study certain properties of interacting particle systems. These systems are important in probability and statistical physics. We consider their long-time behavior and we give some conditions under which they converge. As a key step, we compute a spectral gap in a special case. We also discuss some examples.

What goes wrong:

- It opens with "we study" and with background the reader already knows.
- "Some properties" and "some conditions" hide the actual result.
- "Give", "compute" and "discuss" are weak verbs.
- A real computation is presented as a mere step.

> **After.** We prove that a broad class of interacting particle systems on finite graphs converges to equilibrium exponentially fast, with a rate that does not depend on the size of the graph. We determine the optimal rate on complete graphs and on cycles, and we show that the uniform bound fails without the locality assumption by constructing explicit counterexamples. As an application, we obtain sharp mixing estimates for two classical models of opinion dynamics.

Every sentence now states a result. The reader knows in ten seconds what the paper contains.

## Checklist

- [ ] The first sentence states the main result.
- [ ] All main contributions appear, including the one in the title.
- [ ] Verbs are strong and precise.
- [ ] No symbols, formulas or citations.
- [ ] No result is presented as a mere tool or as a special case.
- [ ] Every claim is proved in the paper.
- [ ] One paragraph, within the journal's word limit.

## The title

The same rules apply in a few words. Name the objects and the type of result: "Classification of …", "Rigidity of …", "Integration of … by …". Avoid titles that are questions or jokes, and avoid "On some properties of …", which says nothing. A good title contains the words that a researcher in your area would type into a search engine.

guides.title: Writing the introduction, the motivation and the contribution
guides.summary: An introduction tells a short story. Where the problem comes from, why it matters, what was missing, and what this paper adds, with the main results stated early and the proofs kept for later.
guides.body:
The introduction is where the paper is accepted or rejected. A referee forms an opinion in the first two pages. A reader decides whether to continue. It must position the problem, motivate it, and make the contribution impossible to miss.

## The arc of a good introduction

1. **Context and history.** Where does the problem come from? Who introduced the objects, and what was known? A few sentences of history give the reader a frame. Do not cut them to save space.
2. **Motivation.** Why does the question matter? What does it unlock, what does it explain, which open problem does it touch? This is the *why* of the paper, and it must be explicit.
3. **The gap.** What was missing before this paper? Be fair to earlier work. The gap is what nobody had done, not what others did badly.
4. **The main contribution.** State it early, ideally on the first or second page. If the paper has one main theorem, it should appear before the reader has to turn too many pages.
5. **The other results.** Describe the contribution of each part of the paper in general terms. Not every result needs to be stated in full in the introduction.
6. **Organization of the paper.** A short paragraph at the end, one sentence per section.
7. **Acknowledgments.** Thank the people and institutions who helped.

## Stating the main results

- **Label the main results** Theorem A, Theorem B, Theorem C in the introduction, so they are easy to cite and easy to find. Keep the numbered Theorem, Proposition and Lemma environments for the body.
- **Define everything first.** Every object and every symbol in Theorem A must be defined before Theorem A. Introduce the objects in the prose that leads to the theorem.
- **Never mention a theorem before stating it.** Do not write "Theorem B below shows…" in the first paragraph. State Theorem B, then discuss it.
- **Keep statements minimal.** The statement should contain the hypotheses and the conclusion, nothing else. Interpretations, special cases and remarks go in the prose right after the statement.
- **Keep the subtleties for later.** Sign conventions, technical normalizations and degenerate cases belong to the definitions in the body. The introduction states the clean version.

## What to leave out

- **Details of the proofs.** One or two sentences on the main idea of a proof are welcome when the idea is itself new. A step-by-step account of the proof is not. It belongs to the body.
- **Long lists of internal references.** "By Lemma 3.4, Proposition 4.2 and Corollary 5.7" makes the introduction unreadable. The reader has not seen these yet.
- **Every reference you know.** Cite what is essential to position the problem and what the paper actually uses. An introduction is not a survey.
- **Thematic subsections.** A research introduction usually reads best as continuous prose, with only the final "Organization" and "Acknowledgments" as separate headings.
- **The same first sentence as in your last three papers.** If every introduction you write opens with "X, introduced by Y in 19…, have been widely studied", change it. Open with the question, a striking example, or the reason the problem matters now.

## The motivation paragraph

A motivation paragraph answers *why should anyone care?* Three good answers:

- **It solves or advances a known problem**: an open question, a conjecture, a gap explicitly mentioned in the literature. Cite where it was asked.
- **It connects two areas**: the result lets methods from one field act on another.
- **It explains a phenomenon**: it shows why a family of known examples behaves the way it does.

A bad answer is "this has not been studied before". Many things have not been studied, for good reasons.

## Selling the paper, honestly

The introduction must sell the paper, but with mathematical honesty. Say clearly what is new. If your theorem extends a known result, explain what the extension adds: more generality, a new method, a sharp bound, a counterexample showing the hypotheses are needed. Do not make your results look like routine special cases, and do not claim more than you prove.

## Checklist

- [ ] The first page says what the problem is and why it matters.
- [ ] The history is short but present.
- [ ] The main result appears early.
- [ ] Every object in a main theorem is defined before it.
- [ ] No theorem is mentioned before it is stated.
- [ ] No proof is explained in detail.
- [ ] Only essential references are cited.
- [ ] The last paragraphs are "Organization of the paper" and "Acknowledgments".

guides.title: Presenting results and proofs
guides.summary: How to organize sections, choose between Theorem, Proposition and Lemma, write proofs that read as prose, display equations, and keep the LaTeX source clean.
guides.body:
A paper can contain excellent results and still be hard to read because of how they are presented. Structure is not decoration. It tells the reader what matters, where to find it and what can be skipped.

## Sections

- **Few sections, each with one job.** A typical research paper has an introduction, a section of preliminaries, two to four sections of results, and sometimes a section of examples. Short papers can do with three sections in total.
- **Name sections after objects or tools**: "Graded modules and their duals", "The blow-up groupoid", "A spectral sequence". Do not title a section "Proof of Theorem A". The title should tell the reader what the section is about.
- **Open each section with its goal.** One or two sentences: "In this section, we construct… The main result is Proposition 3.5, which is the key input in the proof of Theorem B." The reader knows immediately why the section is there.

## Theorem, Proposition, Lemma, Corollary

Use the environments as a hierarchy, not as decoration.

- **Theorem** for the main results of the paper, the ones announced in the introduction. Usually two to four in a paper.
- **Proposition** for important results of the paper that are not main results.
- **Lemma** for technical steps used in proofs.
- **Corollary** for direct consequences of a theorem or a proposition.
- **Remark** and **Example** for comments and illustrations that are not used in proofs.

If every result is a Theorem, nothing stands out. A standard or easy fact does not need an environment at all: state it in a sentence in the text, with a short justification.

**Results from the literature are cited, not restated.** If you use a known result, write "by [8, Theorem 2.1], the map is an isomorphism". Do not restate it as "Proposition 2.3 ([8])" and do not reprove it. Keep the paper focused on what is new.

## Writing proofs

- **Continuous prose.** Write proofs as connected paragraphs, not as "Step 1, Step 2, Step 3". If a proof is long, split it into lemmas with clear statements, then the proof of the theorem becomes short and readable.
- **Announce the strategy.** For a long proof, the first sentence says how it goes: "We argue by induction on the length", "The proof reduces to the case of a point, which we treat with a local model".
- **Make the main proofs easy to find.** When the proof of a main theorem comes much later than its statement, give it a visible heading: **Proof of Theorem B.** in bold. A reader looking for it should find it in seconds.
- **Be exact about what is used.** Each step should be justified by a precise reference: an earlier equation, a numbered lemma, or an exact citation.

## Displayed equations

- **Display the important equations.** Center the key formulas on their own lines. Inline formulas should be short.
- **Number only what you refer to.** An equation needs a number only if the text cites it later. Unnumbered displays are cleaner.
- **Punctuate equations.** A displayed equation is part of a sentence. End it with a comma or a period when the sentence requires it.
- **Align multi-line computations** on the relation symbol, so the reader follows the chain of equalities.

## Notation

- Introduce all notation in one place when possible, usually the preliminaries.
- Use standard symbols for standard objects. Use simple letters ($U$, $V$, $W$ for open sets, $f$, $g$ for maps) and keep fancy alphabets for genuinely different types of objects.
- Never use the same symbol for two different things, and never change the symbol of an object halfway through the paper.

## Figures

Figures are often the fastest way to explain a construction. Keep captions short, one line if possible, and put the explanation in the text that cites the figure. Use the same colors and conventions in all figures of the paper.

## Length

Clarity is worth a few pages. A 20-page paper that a referee reads in one afternoon is better than a 12-page paper that takes a week to decode. Do not condense to the point of losing the reader.

## LaTeX habits that editors notice

- **Use a standard class** (for example `amsart` in mathematics) and the journal's class only at the end, when the paper is accepted.
- **Write references with their name**: `Lemma~\ref{...}` or `Lemma \ref{...}`. Avoid packages that cause trouble on arXiv. Check that the source compiles on arXiv before submitting.
- **Use meaningful or stable labels** and never reuse a label.
- **One bibliography style** for the whole paper, with complete entries: authors, title, journal, volume, year, pages, DOI or arXiv number.
- **Clean the source before posting.** Remove commented-out paragraphs, private notes and unused packages. arXiv makes the source public.
- **Do not fight the class.** Avoid manual spacing such as `\vspace` and `\\` to adjust the layout. Let LaTeX do the typesetting.

## Checklist

- [ ] Sections are named after objects, and each opens with its goal.
- [ ] Theorem is reserved for the main results.
- [ ] Known results are cited with exact numbers, not reproved.
- [ ] Proofs are in prose, and main proofs have bold headings.
- [ ] Only referenced equations are numbered.
- [ ] Notation is introduced once and never changes.
- [ ] The source is clean and compiles on arXiv.

guides.title: Revising paragraphs, step by step
guides.summary: A method to revise a paragraph without losing your voice. Check the content first, then the structure, then the sentences, then the words. Keep your notation and your structure intact.
guides.body:
Most of the quality of a paper comes from revision. The first draft says what you mean. The revision makes the reader understand it. Revise in passes, from the largest scale to the smallest, and do one thing at a time.

## Pass 1: is it correct?

Before improving a single sentence, check the mathematics or the science.

- Is every claim true as stated, with all hypotheses?
- Is every step justified, by a proof or by an exact reference?
- Are the definitions used exactly as they were defined?

There is no point in polishing a wrong sentence. When you revise someone else's text, this is also where your main responsibility lies: correct the content, and only then the language.

## Pass 2: what is the paragraph for?

A paragraph has one job. Write that job in a few words in the margin: "defines the map", "explains why the hypothesis is needed", "states the main result". If you cannot, the paragraph does two things and should be split. If two consecutive paragraphs have the same job, merge them.

The first sentence of a paragraph should announce its job. The reader who only reads first sentences should still follow the argument.

## Pass 3: sentences

- **One idea per sentence.** Split long sentences at "and", "which" and "where".
- **Periods, not semicolons.** A semicolon usually joins two sentences that would be clearer apart.
- **Put the new information at the end.** "The map $f$ is injective" when $f$ is known. "There is a unique injective map, which we denote by $f$" when $f$ is new.
- **Prefer the active voice.** "We prove" rather than "it is proved".
- **Keep related words together.** Do not put a long clause between the subject and the verb.

## Pass 4: words

Cut words that carry no information:

| Instead of | Write |
|---|---|
| It is worth noting that $X$ | $X$ |
| In order to | To |
| Due to the fact that | Because |
| A number of | Several, or the exact number |
| It can be shown that $X$ | $X$, followed by the proof or a reference |
| Plays a crucial role in | Is used in, or say exactly how |
| In this regard, moreover, furthermore | Often nothing at all |

Watch for vague words: *certain, some, various, interesting, important*. Replace them by the precise object or property.

## What not to change

When you revise your own text after some time, or a co-author's text, keep what works:

- **Keep the notation.** Changing notation during revision introduces errors everywhere else in the paper.
- **Keep the structure** of sections and results unless it is wrong. Revision improves sentences, it is not a rewrite.
- **Keep the author's voice.** The goal is clarity, not a different style. A paragraph should still sound like its author after revision.

## An example

The paragraph below is invented.

> **Before.** It is worth noting that, in order to prove the main result, which plays a crucial role in Section 4, we will need a certain number of preliminary results; in particular, we will need to show that the operator $T$, which was defined in Section 2 and which is bounded, has a closed range, and this will be done by using a compactness argument.

> **After.** The main result needs one preliminary fact. The operator $T$ of Section 2 has closed range. We prove this with a compactness argument.

The content is the same. The revised version has three sentences, one idea each, and no empty phrase.

## Read aloud

The last pass is to read the paragraph aloud, slowly. You will hear the sentences that are too long, the repeated words and the missing transitions. If you run out of breath, the sentence is too long.

## Checklist

- [ ] The content is correct and every step is justified.
- [ ] Each paragraph has one job, announced in its first sentence.
- [ ] Each sentence has one idea.
- [ ] Empty phrases and vague words are gone.
- [ ] Notation and structure are unchanged.
- [ ] The paragraph reads well aloud.

guides.title: Choosing a journal
guides.summary: Scope first, then level, then the editor. What Q1 and Q2 really mean, how to read an editorial board, how to recognize a predatory journal, and how to build a realistic list of targets.
guides.body:
Choosing a journal is a strategic decision. A good choice gives a fair review by people who understand the work and a publication that the right readers will see. A bad choice costs months: a desk rejection, a referee outside the field, or a paper lost in a journal nobody reads.

## Step 1: scope

The first question is not "how good is the journal?" but "does this journal publish papers like mine?"

- **Read the aims and scope** on the journal's page.
- **Look at the last two years of issues.** Are there papers on your topic, with your methods?
- **Look at your own bibliography.** Where were the papers you cite most published? Those journals already have editors and referees for your area.

A paper outside a journal's scope is often rejected by the editor without review, however good it is.

## Step 2: level

Be honest about the significance of your result. Ask a senior colleague or your supervisor. A useful way to think:

- **Top general journals** publish results that matter to a wide part of the discipline.
- **Strong specialized journals** publish important results within one area.
- **Good solid journals** publish correct, useful, new results with a narrower audience.

Aim one notch higher than your first instinct, not three. A realistic ladder of three journals, decided before the first submission, saves time after a rejection.

## What Q1, Q2, Q3 and Q4 mean

Quartiles rank journals *within a subject category* by a citation indicator.

- **Q1** means the journal is in the top 25% of its category, **Q2** in the next 25%, and so on.
- The two common sources are **SCImago Journal Rank** (SJR, free, at scimagojr.com, based on Scopus data) and Clarivate's **Journal Citation Reports** (JCR, by subscription, based on the Journal Impact Factor).
- The same journal can be Q1 in one category and Q2 in another, and can have different quartiles in SJR and JCR. Always say which ranking you use.
- Quartiles change every year.

**Use quartiles carefully.** They measure citations, and citation habits vary enormously between fields. In mathematics, papers are cited slowly and over decades, so citation metrics are weak signals. Mathematicians also look at MathSciNet's Mathematical Citation Quotient (MCQ) and above all at the reputation of the journal among specialists. Your institution or funding agency may require Q1 or Q2 publications. Know the rule, but choose the journal for its readers, not only for its quartile.

## Step 3: the editor

The editor-in-chief usually does not handle your paper personally. A member of the editorial board does: the *handling editor*, sometimes called associate editor. This person chooses the referees and makes the recommendation.

- **Read the editorial board.** Is there at least one editor whose own research is close to your paper? If nobody on the board works in your area, the journal is probably not the right one.
- **Some journals ask you to choose or suggest an editor.** Choose the board member whose recent papers are closest to yours, not the most famous one.
- **Suggested referees.** Many journals let you suggest referees. Suggest experts without conflicts of interest: no co-authors, no colleagues from your institution, no close collaborators.

## Step 4: practical criteria

- **Review time.** Some journals publish median times from submission to decision. In mathematics, a full review often takes several months and can take more than a year.
- **Open access and fees.** *Diamond* open access journals charge neither readers nor authors. *Gold* open access journals charge an article processing charge (APC). Subscription journals are free for authors and usually allow you to keep the preprint on arXiv. Check the journal's copyright and preprint policy.
- **Indexing.** Check that the journal is indexed where your field looks: Web of Science, Scopus, zbMATH Open and MathSciNet for mathematics, PubMed for life sciences.
- **Length and format limits.** Some journals have page limits or require a specific template.

## Recognizing a predatory journal

Predatory journals charge fees and publish almost anything, with little or no real review. They damage a CV. Warning signs:

- An unsolicited email inviting you to submit, often flattering, often outside your field.
- A promise of very fast acceptance, "peer review in 7 days".
- A broad, vague scope ("International Journal of Advanced Science and Research").
- Fees announced only after acceptance, or hard to find.
- An editorial board that is hard to verify, or names used without consent.
- Invented metrics ("Global Impact Factor").

Use the checklist at **thinkchecksubmit.org**. For open access journals, check that the journal is listed in the **Directory of Open Access Journals** (doaj.org). Ask your supervisor or librarian when in doubt.

## Rules you must follow

- **One journal at a time.** Submitting the same paper to two journals simultaneously is not allowed.
- **Posting on arXiv** before or during submission is accepted by most journals in mathematics, physics and computer science. Check the policy of your target journal.
- **After a rejection**, read the reports, improve the paper, and submit to the next journal on your list. Do not send the same version again.

## Checklist

- [ ] The journal publishes papers like mine, in the last two years.
- [ ] The level matches the significance of the result.
- [ ] At least one editor works in my area.
- [ ] The journal is indexed and is not predatory.
- [ ] I know its fees, preprint policy and typical review time.
- [ ] I have a list of three journals, in order.

guides.title: Submission, cover letters and peer review
guides.summary: What to check before submitting, how to write a short cover letter, what happens during review, and how to answer referees point by point. Also how to write a referee report yourself.
guides.body:
Submitting a paper is the start of a conversation with an editor and one or more referees. It usually lasts months. A clean submission and calm, precise answers make it shorter.

## Before you submit

- **Read the paper one last time on paper**, from the title to the last reference.
- **Ask a colleague** who did not write it to read the abstract and the introduction. If they cannot say what the main result is, revise.
- **Post the preprint** on arXiv if your field does so and the journal allows it. It establishes the date of your result and makes it visible.
- **Prepare the files**: the PDF, the LaTeX source if required, figures, and the list of suggested referees if the journal asks for one.
- **Check the author information**: full names, affiliations, institutional email addresses, ORCID identifiers, and funding acknowledgments.

## The cover letter

Keep it short: three or four paragraphs, one page at most. The editor reads many of them.

1. **What you submit**: the title, the authors and the journal.
2. **What the paper does**: the main result in two or three sentences, in words, as in the abstract.
3. **Why this journal**: one sentence linking the paper to the journal's scope or to papers it published.
4. **Formalities**: the paper is not under consideration elsewhere, the preprint is on arXiv (with its number), and the suggested editor or referees if relevant.

> Dear Editor,
>
> We submit our paper "…" for consideration in *[Journal]*. In this paper, we prove that … We also show that … and, as an application, we …
>
> The paper continues a line of work published in *[Journal]*, notably [reference]. The manuscript is not under consideration elsewhere. A preprint is available as arXiv:XXXX.XXXXX.
>
> Sincerely, …

## What happens next

1. **Editorial screening.** The editor checks the scope and the general level. A *desk rejection* at this stage is common and often fast. It is not a judgment on correctness.
2. **Referees.** The handling editor invites one or more referees. Finding them can itself take weeks.
3. **Reports.** Referees read the paper and write reports. This is the long part.
4. **Decision**: accept (rare at the first round), minor revision, major revision, or reject.

You can politely ask the editorial office about the status after a reasonable time, for example after six months without news in a slow field. One short, courteous email is enough.

## Answering the referees

A revision is accepted when the referees see that every point was taken seriously.

- **Thank the referees once**, briefly, at the start. Not in every answer.
- **Answer point by point.** Copy each comment, then write your answer under it. Say exactly what you changed and where: "We added Remark 3.4 on page 9", "The proof of Lemma 2.1 now treats the case $n = 0$ separately".
- **Change the paper, not only the letter.** If a referee misunderstood a passage, the passage probably needs rewriting. Other readers will misunderstand it too.
- **Disagree politely, with arguments.** You do not have to accept every suggestion. If you disagree, explain why, with a precise mathematical or scientific reason. Never be sarcastic.
- **Mark the changes.** Send a version with the changes highlighted, or a list of changes, if the journal allows it.

> **Comment 3.** The assumption that $X$ is compact seems unnecessary in Theorem B.
>
> **Answer.** We agree that it is not needed for the existence part. It is needed for uniqueness: Example 5.2 (new) gives two non-isomorphic solutions on a non-compact $X$. We have split Theorem B into two statements accordingly, see page 4.

## After a rejection

A rejection is part of the job, even for the best researchers. Wait a day before reading the reports again. Extract every useful comment, improve the paper, and submit to the next journal on your list.

## Writing a referee report yourself

Sooner or later, you will be asked to referee. A good report is precise and useful to both the editor and the authors.

1. **Summary**: what the paper claims, in your own words, in one paragraph. This shows the editor you understood it.
2. **Assessment**: is it correct, new, and significant for this journal? Give reasons.
3. **Major comments**: errors, gaps in proofs, missing references, overstated claims.
4. **Minor comments**: typos, unclear sentences, notation, listed by page and line.
5. **Recommendation**, in a separate confidential note to the editor if the journal allows it.

Be kind and specific. Criticize the paper, never the authors. If you cannot assess part of the paper, say so to the editor. Decline the invitation if you have a conflict of interest or no time to do it properly.

## Checklist

- [ ] Preprint posted, files and author information ready.
- [ ] Cover letter of one page with the main result in words.
- [ ] Answers to referees point by point, with the exact changes.
- [ ] Disagreements explained with arguments, never with irritation.

guides.title: A research method, from the first idea to the preprint
guides.summary: Choosing a problem, working in examples, discussing the strategy before writing proofs, checking originality, keeping a research log, and writing to other researchers about their work.
guides.body:
Research is not a straight line from idea to paper. It is a cycle: read, try, fail, understand, try again. A method does not make the ideas come, but it makes sure that good ideas are not lost and that bad ones are abandoned early.

## 1. Choose a problem you can finish

A good first problem is precise, connected to active work, and small enough to finish in a few months. Good sources:

- **Questions stated explicitly** in recent papers, often in the introduction or in a final section on open problems.
- **A known result in a special case** that nobody has extended. Ask why: sometimes it is hard, sometimes nobody tried.
- **A hypothesis that a proof uses only once.** Can it be weakened?
- **Two areas that use the same objects** with different methods.

Write the problem down in one sentence. If you cannot, it is not yet a problem.

## 2. Work in examples first

Before looking for a general proof, compute the smallest non-trivial examples by hand, and the next ones with a computer if needed. Examples tell you whether the statement is true, which hypotheses are needed, and often how the proof should go. A counterexample found in the first week is a gift.

## 3. Discuss the strategy before writing proofs

When you believe you have a proof, do not write it in full LaTeX yet. Write a half-page outline:

- the statement, with all hypotheses,
- the two or three key steps,
- the known results each step uses, with exact references,
- the step you are least sure about.

Discuss this outline with your supervisor or co-authors. Most mistakes are found at this stage, cheaply. Write the formal proof only once the strategy has survived the discussion.

## 4. Check originality early and honestly

Before investing months, check that the result is not already known.

- Search arXiv, Google Scholar and the reviewing databases with several formulations of the statement.
- Read the papers that cite the closest known results.
- Ask an expert.

Separate two questions that are often confused:

1. **Does a statement of this form already exist in the literature?** If no paper contains it, the result is new, even if its proof combines known ingredients.
2. **How difficult is the proof, and what does it use?** A short proof from known tools can still be a new and useful result. Be honest about it in the introduction.

## 5. Keep a research log

Keep a dated log of what you tried, what failed and why. Failed approaches are information: they tell you, and later your readers, why the obvious method does not work. A simple text file or notebook is enough. Keep with it your reading sheets and a list of open questions.

A tool such as [VanoAtlas](https://github.com/yassine-aitmohamed/vanoatlas) can hold projects, tasks, meetings, notes and papers in one private place on your computer, but any consistent system works. The point is to write things down the day they happen.

## 6. Meet regularly

A short weekly meeting with your supervisor or co-authors, prepared in advance, is worth more than a long meeting every two months. Bring one page: what you did, what is blocked, what you plan next, and one precise question.

## 7. Writing to other researchers about their work

Writing to the author of a paper is normal and often welcome: to ask a question, to report a possible problem, or to share an application of their result. A good email is short, kind and concrete.

- **Start with their work, not with yourself.** "I recently read your paper '…' with great interest." Your email address and signature already say who you are.
- **Start from a concrete example.** Explain that you tried to apply their result to a specific case. Put the detailed computation in a short PDF attached to the email, without title page or sections, just the example.
- **Phrase observations humbly.** "If I compute correctly, …", "I may be missing something, but …". Never write as if their work were wrong, even when you think there is an error. You may be the one who is mistaken, and if not, they will appreciate the courtesy.
- **Ask one clear question** in the body of the email.
- **Keep it short.** A few paragraphs. Formulas in simple LaTeX notation are fine.

> Dear Professor …,
>
> I recently read your paper "…" with great interest. I tried to apply Theorem 3.1 to the case of …, and I attach a short note with the computation.
>
> If I compute correctly, the condition (2.4) fails in this example, while the conclusion of the theorem seems to hold. I may be missing something in the hypotheses. Could the condition be replaced by …, or is there a reason it is needed here?
>
> Thank you very much for your time.
>
> Best regards, …

## 8. Read and review as training

Writing short reviews of recent papers (for example for zbMATH Open or MathSciNet in mathematics) and refereeing for journals are excellent training. You learn to read fast, to identify the main contribution of a paper in a few lines, and to see the common weaknesses that you will then avoid in your own papers.

## 9. Finish

A finished, correct, modest paper is worth more than a brilliant unfinished one. Set a date, write the paper, post the preprint, and start the next project while the first one is under review.

## In short

- [ ] The problem fits in one precise sentence.
- [ ] The smallest examples are computed by hand.
- [ ] The strategy is discussed before any formal proof is written.
- [ ] Originality is checked, and kept separate from difficulty.
- [ ] A dated research log records what failed and why.
- [ ] Emails to other researchers are short, concrete and humble.
- [ ] The paper is finished and posted, and the next project has started.

guides.title: Finding a PhD abroad
guides.summary: How doctoral admission works in the main systems, where funded positions are advertised, and a twelve-month plan from the first search to the first day in a new country.
guides.body:
A PhD abroad changes a career. It gives you new supervisors, a new network and often better funding. It also takes more planning than most students expect. The first thing to understand is that there is no single "PhD application". Each country, and sometimes each university, recruits doctoral students in its own way.

## Two ways of recruiting doctoral students

**1. Position-based (like a job).** A professor or a project has funding for one doctoral researcher on a defined topic. The position is advertised, you apply with a CV and a letter, and the best candidate is hired, often with an employment contract and a salary. This is common in Germany, the Netherlands, the Nordic countries, Switzerland, and in projects funded by the European Union.

**2. Programme-based (like an admission).** A department admits a cohort of students each year through a committee. You apply to the programme, not to a person, and you choose your supervisor later. Funding usually comes from teaching or research assistantships. This is the standard model in the United States.

Many countries mix the two. In **Canada**, you apply to a department, but in research-based programmes admission often depends on a professor agreeing to supervise you, so contacting supervisors early is essential. In **France**, doctoral contracts are awarded through competitions run by doctoral schools, usually for a topic proposed by a supervisor. In the **United Kingdom**, most funded places are "studentships" attached to a project or a doctoral training centre.

## The main systems at a glance

| Country | Typical length | How you get in | How it is funded |
|---|---|---|---|
| United States | 5 to 6 years | Apply to a department programme, deadlines usually December to January | Teaching or research assistantships, fellowships |
| Canada | 4 to 5 years | Apply to a department, often with a supervisor's agreement | Supervisor's grants, teaching, university and federal scholarships |
| United Kingdom | 3 to 4 years | Apply to an advertised studentship or a training centre | Studentships from research councils or universities |
| France | 3 years | Apply to a thesis topic, then the doctoral school competition | Doctoral contract (a salaried 3-year contract), CIFRE with a company |
| Germany | 3 to 4 years | Apply to an advertised position or a structured programme | Employment contract on a project, or a scholarship |
| Netherlands, Nordics, Switzerland | 3 to 5 years | Apply to an advertised position | Employment contract with a salary |

The table gives typical patterns. Details vary between universities, so always check the doctoral school's own page.

## Where funded positions are advertised

- **EURAXESS** (euraxess.ec.europa.eu): the European Commission's portal for research jobs, including PhD positions across Europe and positions funded by the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions. You can filter by field, country and funding, and save searches with email alerts.
- **FindAPhD** (findaphd.com) and **jobs.ac.uk**: the main listings for the United Kingdom, with many international positions.
- **DAAD** (daad.de): the German Academic Exchange Service lists international doctoral programmes and its own scholarships. PhDGermany lists open doctoral positions.
- **ADUM** (adum.fr): the portal used by many French doctoral schools to publish thesis topics and receive applications.
- **AcademicPositions** (academicpositions.com): research jobs in Europe and beyond.
- **Department and research-group pages**: many positions are only posted there. Follow the groups you are interested in.
- **Mailing lists and societies** of your field, which often circulate PhD offers.

## A twelve-month plan

**12 to 9 months before the start.** Decide on two or three countries and your research area. Read recent papers in that area and list the people who wrote them. Check language requirements and test dates (for example English tests).

**9 to 6 months before.** Contact potential supervisors (see [Contacting a professor](contacting-a-professor.html)). Prepare your CV, a statement of purpose and, where needed, a research proposal (see [The PhD application file](phd-application-documents.html)). Ask your referees early.

**6 to 3 months before.** Apply. Programme deadlines in the United States and Canada are often in December or January for a September start. European positions open all year. French doctoral contract competitions usually happen in spring and early summer.

**3 to 0 months before.** Interviews, offers, the visa, health insurance, accommodation. EURAXESS also has practical pages on moving to Europe as a researcher.

## Questions to ask before accepting an offer

- What exactly is the funding, for how long, and what happens if the thesis takes longer?
- Is there teaching, and how many hours?
- Who is the supervisor, and how often will you meet?
- Is there a doctoral school with courses, seminars and a thesis committee?
- What is the cost of living compared with the salary or stipend?

The guide [Choosing a supervisor](choosing-a-supervisor.html) explains how to evaluate the person you will work with for several years.

## Checklist

- [ ] I know which recruitment model each target country uses.
- [ ] I have a list of supervisors and groups whose recent papers I have read.
- [ ] I have saved searches on EURAXESS and the national portals.
- [ ] My CV, statement and proposal are ready, and my referees are informed.
- [ ] I know the deadlines, the language requirements and the visa steps.

guides.title: Contacting a professor
guides.summary: How to write the first email to a potential supervisor or collaborator, what to attach, when to follow up, and the mistakes that send an email straight to the archive.
guides.body:
Professors receive many emails from prospective students, and most of them look the same: a long paragraph about passion, a list of grades, and a request for "any opportunity". These are rarely answered. A short, specific email that shows you have read the professor's work has a much better chance.

## Before you write

1. **Read two or three recent papers** of the professor, at least the abstract and the introduction (see [How to read a research paper](reading-a-paper.html)).
2. **Check the group's page** for open positions, instructions for prospective students, and the professor's current students.
3. **Check whether the professor can supervise**: some are retired, on leave, or not taking students this year. The page often says so.
4. **Know the admission route** of the country (see [Finding a PhD abroad](finding-a-phd-abroad.html)). In some systems, an email to a professor is essential. In others, the professor will simply tell you to apply to the programme.

## The structure of a good first email

**Subject line.** Make it specific: "Prospective PhD student: your work on [topic]" or "Application for the PhD position [reference]". Never "Request" or "Hello Professor".

**First paragraph: who you are, in one sentence.** Your current degree and university, and what you are looking for. "I am finishing a master's degree in mathematics at [University], and I am looking for a PhD position starting in September [year]."

**Second paragraph: why this professor.** Name one or two specific papers and say what interested you, in your own words. Connect it to what you have done: your thesis, a project, a course. This paragraph is the reason the email gets answered.

**Third paragraph: what you bring.** Two or three concrete facts: your master's thesis topic, a preprint, a relevant skill, a scholarship you hold or will apply for. Not a list of every course.

**Fourth paragraph: the request.** Ask one clear question. "Would you consider supervising a PhD student in this direction, and if so, is there an application route you would recommend?"

**Attachments.** A one or two-page CV in PDF and, if you have one, your master's thesis or a writing sample. Name files clearly: `Lastname_CV.pdf`.

## An example

> **Subject:** Prospective PhD student: your work on [topic]
>
> Dear Professor [Name],
>
> I am completing a master's degree in mathematics at [University] and I am looking for a PhD position starting in September [year].
>
> I recently read your paper "[Title]" with great interest, in particular the construction in Section 3, which relates [idea] to [idea]. My master's thesis studies [topic], and I would be very interested in understanding whether a similar approach applies to [question].
>
> In my thesis I proved [one concrete result], and I am comfortable with [relevant tools]. I attach my CV and a draft of my thesis.
>
> Would you consider supervising a PhD student in this direction? If so, I would be grateful for any advice on the application process.
>
> Kind regards,
> [Name]

The example is a template. The point is the structure: specific, short, and honest.

## Follow-up

If there is no answer after two weeks, send one short, polite reminder in the same thread. If there is still no answer after another two weeks, move on. Silence is common and usually means the professor is busy, not that you did something wrong.

## Mistakes that guarantee silence

- A generic email sent to dozens of professors with only the name changed. Professors notice.
- Wrong name, wrong field, or "Dear Sir/Madam".
- Long paragraphs about your passion with no concrete information.
- Asking the professor to read a long proposal before any contact.
- Attachments that are not PDF, or ten attachments.
- Several emails to the same professor in a few days, or emails to everyone in the department at once.

## After a positive answer

A professor who answers positively may suggest a video call. Prepare it like a short interview: be ready to explain your thesis in five minutes, and prepare questions about the group (see [Choosing a supervisor](choosing-a-supervisor.html)). Ask about funding directly and politely. It is a normal question.

## Writing to a researcher about a paper

The same principles apply when you write to an author with a question about their paper: start from their work, give a concrete example, phrase observations humbly, and ask one clear question. The guide [A research method](research-methodology.html) includes a model email.

## Checklist

- [ ] I have read recent papers of the professor and checked the group's page.
- [ ] The subject line is specific.
- [ ] The email names a specific paper and connects it to my own work.
- [ ] It contains one clear question.
- [ ] My CV is attached as a short PDF with a clear file name.
- [ ] I follow up once, after two weeks, and then move on.

guides.title: Choosing a supervisor
guides.summary: The supervisor matters more than the university name. What to look for, the questions to ask, how to talk to current students, and the warning signs to take seriously.
guides.body:
For three to six years, your supervisor will shape your daily work, your first papers, your network and your first job. A brilliant researcher can be a poor supervisor, and a less famous one can be an excellent mentor. Choose the person, not only the topic or the university.

## What to look for

**Research fit.** You should find the supervisor's recent papers interesting enough to read them without being asked. Look at the last five years, not the most famous paper from twenty years ago.

**Active research.** Does the supervisor still publish, give talks, and have current students and postdocs? An active researcher brings you into an active network.

**Track record with students.** Look at former students: did they finish, did they publish, where did they go next? Many group pages list alumni. In mathematics, the Mathematics Genealogy Project lists most supervisors' former students.

**Supervision style.** Some supervisors give a precise problem and meet every week. Others expect you to find your own problem and meet once a month. Neither is wrong. What matters is that the style fits you, especially in the first year.

**Availability.** A supervisor with twenty students or major administrative duties may have little time. Ask how often students meet the supervisor.

**Funding and stability.** Is your funding secure for the whole thesis? Is the supervisor planning to move, retire or take long leave?

**Group and environment.** Are there other students, a seminar, a reading group? A good environment matters as much as the supervisor.

## Questions to ask the supervisor

- What kind of problem would I work on in the first year?
- How often do you meet your students, and how?
- Do your students write papers alone, with you, or both?
- How do you decide authorship on joint papers?
- What do your former students do now?
- What do you expect from a student in the first months?
- How is the funding organised, and what happens if the thesis takes longer?

Ask them calmly. A good supervisor is glad to answer.

## Talk to current students

This is the most useful step, and the one most applicants skip. Write to one or two current or former students (their emails are usually on the department page) and ask for a short call. Ask:

- How often do you meet, and are the meetings useful?
- Do you feel free to ask questions, including basic ones?
- How long do students usually take to finish?
- Would you choose the same supervisor again?

Students are usually honest in a private conversation. Listen to what they do not say as well.

## Warning signs

- Several former students left without finishing, with no clear explanation.
- Current students are vague or uncomfortable when you ask about supervision.
- The supervisor cannot explain what you would work on, or promises everything.
- Authorship conventions are unclear, or students' work is published without them.
- Funding is described as "probably available".
- You leave the conversation feeling small or ignored.

One warning sign is not a verdict. Several are.

## Co-supervision

Many theses have two supervisors: a main one and a second one, sometimes in another university or country (for example in a cotutelle). Co-supervision gives you two perspectives and a wider network. It works well when the roles are clear from the beginning: who you meet weekly, who reads drafts, who decides on the thesis topic.

## Your side of the relationship

A good supervision is a relationship in both directions. Come to meetings prepared, with one page of notes and precise questions. Send drafts early. Say when you are stuck. Keep a written record of what was decided. The guide [Managing your PhD](managing-your-phd.html) describes a weekly routine that makes meetings productive.

## Checklist

- [ ] I have read the supervisor's papers from the last five years.
- [ ] I know where former students went and whether they finished.
- [ ] I have asked about meetings, authorship, funding and expectations.
- [ ] I have talked to at least one current or former student.
- [ ] The supervision style fits the way I work.

guides.title: The PhD application file
guides.summary: The academic CV, the statement of purpose, the research proposal, the letters of recommendation and the interview. What each document is for, and how to make it specific.
guides.body:
A PhD application is read by busy people who compare many files. Each document has one job. The best files are short, specific and consistent: the CV, the statement and the letters tell the same story from different angles.

## The academic CV

An academic CV is not a job CV. It is organized around research and training.

1. **Contact details**: name, email, current position, and links (ORCID, Google Scholar, personal page).
2. **Education**: degrees in reverse order, with the thesis title and supervisor for each research degree.
3. **Research**: preprints and publications in a consistent citation format, then the master's thesis.
4. **Talks and posters**, schools and workshops attended.
5. **Scholarships, awards and prizes.**
6. **Teaching and tutoring**, if any.
7. **Skills**: languages with levels, programming and software actually used.
8. **References**: names, positions and emails of two or three referees.

Keep it to one or two pages at this stage. No photo, no date of birth, unless the country requires them. Use a clean template, for example in LaTeX.

## The statement of purpose

The statement answers three questions: what do you want to work on, why are you prepared for it, and why this place?

- **Open with your research interest**, stated precisely, not with a childhood story.
- **Describe one or two research experiences** in detail: what the question was, what you did, what you learned. Details convince more than adjectives.
- **Explain the fit**: name specific people, groups or seminars at the institution and say why they matter for your project.
- **End with your goal**: what you hope to achieve during the PhD and after.

Typical length: one to two pages. Follow the exact limit and prompt of each programme. Write a new version for each application. A generic statement reads as generic.

## The research proposal

Some systems (for example many in the United Kingdom, Germany and for some scholarships) ask for a research proposal. A good proposal is modest and concrete:

1. **Title** and a short summary.
2. **Background**: what is known, with the essential references.
3. **Question**: the precise problem and why it matters.
4. **Approach**: the methods you will use and why they should work.
5. **Plan**: a realistic timeline, with a first step you could start next month.
6. **References.**

Nobody expects you to know exactly what your thesis will contain. The proposal shows that you can formulate a research question and think about how to attack it. It is also a natural starting point for a conversation with a supervisor.

## Letters of recommendation

Letters often decide the outcome. Choose referees who know your research work, not only your grades: your master's thesis supervisor first, then a professor whose course or project you did well in.

- Ask at least four to six weeks before the deadline.
- Send each referee your CV, your statement, the list of programmes with deadlines, and a short paragraph reminding them of what you did with them.
- Send a polite reminder a week before each deadline.
- Thank them, and tell them the outcome.

## Transcripts, language tests and other documents

Check early whether you need certified translations of transcripts, a degree equivalence, or a language test. These take time. Keep a folder with scanned copies of everything.

## The interview

Many programmes and most advertised positions include an interview, often by video.

- Prepare a five-minute explanation of your master's thesis, for a mathematician who does not know the topic.
- Reread your statement and proposal. Every sentence in them is a possible question.
- Prepare two or three questions of your own about the group and the project.
- Test your camera, microphone and connection. Have a pen and paper ready.
- It is fine to say "I do not know, but I would approach it like this."

## Checklist

- [ ] My CV is research-focused and fits on one or two pages.
- [ ] Each statement is written for the specific programme and names people or groups.
- [ ] My proposal states a precise question and a realistic first step.
- [ ] My referees know my research and have all the information they need.
- [ ] I have checked translations, equivalences and language tests early.
- [ ] I can explain my master's thesis in five minutes.

guides.title: Funding your PhD and finding scholarships
guides.summary: Never start a PhD without funding. The kinds of funding that exist, the main national and international programmes, and how to make a scholarship application stand out.
guides.body:
A PhD is a job. You should be paid for it, through a salary, a stipend or a scholarship that covers your living costs and tuition for the expected length of the thesis. An unfunded PhD is a serious risk to your health, your finances and your research. This guide lists the main kinds of funding and how to look for them.

## Kinds of funding

- **Employment contracts.** You are hired as a doctoral researcher with a salary and social benefits. Common in Germany, the Netherlands, the Nordic countries, Switzerland, and France (the doctoral contract).
- **Assistantships.** A stipend in exchange for teaching (teaching assistant) or research work (research assistant). Standard in the United States and Canada.
- **Studentships.** A stipend plus tuition attached to a project or a training centre. Standard in the United Kingdom.
- **Individual scholarships.** You apply yourself, with a project and a host. They are prestigious and make you more attractive to supervisors.
- **Supervisor's grants.** The supervisor pays you from a research grant, sometimes combined with other sources.

## Programmes worth knowing

The details of each programme change from year to year, so always read the official page before applying.

**Europe**
- **Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA) doctoral networks**: funded PhD positions in European training networks, open to all nationalities, advertised on EURAXESS. They usually require mobility: you must not have lived in the host country for long in the recent past.
- **DAAD scholarships** for doctoral studies in Germany: monthly stipend, insurance and often a language course, for individual projects or structured programmes. The DAAD website lists the programmes and current deadlines.
- **France**: doctoral contracts (three-year salaried contracts, with competitions organized by doctoral schools, often in spring), CIFRE contracts with a company, and scholarships for international students such as France Excellence Eiffel. Topics are published on ADUM and on doctoral school pages.

**Canada**
- Most PhD students are funded by a combination of the supervisor's grants, teaching assistantships and university awards. Ask about the minimum funding package when you are admitted.
- The federal **Canada Graduate Research Scholarship – Doctoral (CGRS-D)** replaced the Vanier scholarships and the former doctoral scholarships of the three federal research councils. Eligibility rules for international students depend on the council and the year, so read the official page.
- **Mitacs Globalink Research Internships** bring senior undergraduate students from partner countries to Canadian universities for a 12-week research project. Former interns can apply for a Globalink Graduate Fellowship if they return for graduate studies.

**United States**
- Admission to a PhD programme in the sciences usually comes with full funding (tuition waiver and stipend) for several years, through assistantships and fellowships.
- External fellowships (for example from national agencies or foundations) are often restricted to citizens or residents. Check before preparing an application.

**Your own country**
Many governments and foundations fund PhDs abroad for their citizens, sometimes with a commitment to return. Ask your university's international office and your ministry of higher education.

## Where to search

- The doctoral school or graduate school page of each target university: it lists internal scholarships and the funding guaranteed to admitted students.
- EURAXESS (funding section), the DAAD database, Campus France, and national research council pages.
- Your professors and alumni of your programme who are now abroad.

## Making a scholarship application stand out

- **Start early.** Many scholarships close a year before the start of the PhD and need a host's agreement first.
- **Follow the evaluation criteria.** Most programmes publish them: academic excellence, quality of the project, fit with the host, potential impact. Make sure each criterion is visibly addressed.
- **Get a strong host letter.** A supervisor who explains why your project fits the group carries a lot of weight.
- **Have the file read** by someone who has won the same scholarship.
- **Apply to several sources** at the same time, when the rules allow it.

## Warning signs

- A PhD "position" that asks you to pay a large fee to an agent or to the university for the position itself.
- Funding for one year only, with vague promises for the rest.
- A stipend far below the local cost of living.

Ask about these points in writing before accepting.

## Checklist

- [ ] I will not start a PhD without funding for its expected length.
- [ ] I know which kind of funding is standard in each target country.
- [ ] I have a list of scholarships with deadlines and eligibility rules.
- [ ] I have checked the official page of each programme for the current year.
- [ ] Each application addresses the published evaluation criteria.

guides.title: Applying for postdoctoral positions
guides.summary: The postdoc job market runs on a yearly calendar. Where positions are posted, what goes in the research statement, how to manage letters, and how to compare offers.
guides.body:
The postdoc is the first independent step of a research career. Applications are prepared during the last year of the PhD, often while you are still writing the thesis. Start planning about eighteen months before your expected defence.

## The calendar

In mathematics and many sciences, the academic job market follows a yearly cycle, especially in North America.

- **Summer, a year before the start**: prepare documents and talk to your supervisor about letter writers.
- **September to December**: most applications. In the United States and Canada, many deadlines fall between November and early January. Some fellowships close as early as October.
- **January to April**: interviews and offers. Many US offers are made between late January and April.
- **Europe**: positions are posted throughout the year, often attached to a specific grant, with shorter and less predictable timelines.

## Where positions are posted

- **MathJobs.org** (run by the American Mathematical Society): the main system for academic mathematics jobs in the United States and Canada, also used by some institutions elsewhere. You create one account, upload documents once, and letter writers upload their letters there.
- **AcademicJobsOnline.org**: used by some institutions and fields.
- **EURAXESS** and national portals for Europe, and the job pages of research institutes.
- **Your network**: many European postdocs on a grant are filled by people the grant holder has met. Talk to researchers at conferences and tell them you are on the market.

## The documents

- **Cover letter**: one page, tailored to each position. Name the people you would like to work with and why.
- **CV and publication list**: preprints with arXiv numbers, accepted papers with journals.
