guides.summary: In some problems the worst parts decide the outcome. In others only the best parts matter. Science is mostly of the second kind, and seeing it that way changes how to choose problems, how to judge others' work and how to spend a career.
guides.body:
The psychologist Adam Mastroianni uses a simple distinction to explain why so much effort in science goes in the wrong direction. Some problems are **weak-link problems**: the result depends on the worst element. Others are **strong-link problems**: the result depends on the best element, and the worst barely matters.

## Two kinds of problems

- **Weak-link problems.** Food safety: one contaminated product can kill. A car engine: the best spark plugs do not help if the gearbox is broken. You solve them by raising the floor, with rules, inspections and standards.
- **Strong-link problems.** Music: you listen to the best albums and ignore the rest. Athletics at the Olympics: only the best athletes count. You solve them by raising the ceiling, by letting many attempts happen and finding the best.

Using the wrong method is costly. Inspecting every song before release would remove the bad music and most of the great music too.

## Why science is a strong-link problem

In the long run, science keeps its best ideas and forgets the rest. Phlogiston, the ether and the theory of tiny humans curled inside sperm cells are gone, while evolution, quantum mechanics and the calculus remain. A thousand forgettable papers do not cancel one paper that changes a field. Bad work can waste time and resources for a while, and fraud does real damage, but what matters most is how good the best work is.

Mastroianni argues that science is often run as if it were a weak-link problem: heavy screening of papers and grants designed above all to stop bad work. Such screening also tends to stop risky, novel and interdisciplinary work, which is where the strongest links come from. Several Nobel laureates, among them Peter Higgs and Sydney Brenner speaking about Frederick Sanger, have said that their work would not survive today's pressure to publish regularly.

## The other side

Not everything in science is a strong-link problem. Fraud, errors in data that others build on, and clinical results that guide treatment are weak-link problems: one bad result can do real harm. Dan Elton's defence of peer review, discussed in [Understanding peer review](understanding-peer-review.html), argues that expert screening also protects fields from spending years on false spectacular claims. The point is not to remove all quality control, but to know which kind of problem you face.

## What it changes for your own work

- **Aim for your best work, not for zero flaws.** Your career will be remembered for its best results. Ten safe papers matter less than one important one.
- **Allow yourself risky projects.** Keep a safe project that will surely produce a paper, and a risky one that might produce something important.
- **Spend little energy policing others.** Pointing out errors that matter is part of science. Spending a career fighting mediocre work changes little. Doing great work changes more.
- **Judge a researcher by their best work.** In hiring, refereeing and collaborating, ask what someone's strongest result is.
- **Know when you face a weak link.** When others will rely on your data, your code or your proof, check it as if one error could ruin everything, because it can.

## Checklist

- [ ] I can name the most important result I am working towards, not only the next paper.
- [ ] I have at least one risky project alongside a safe one.
- [ ] I check with extra care every result that others will build on.
- [ ] When I evaluate others, I look first at their best work.

## Summary

- Weak-link problems depend on the worst element, strong-link problems on the best.
- Science is mostly a strong-link problem: its best ideas last and the rest is forgotten.
- Screening for safety can also remove the most original work.
- Aim high, take some risks, and check carefully what others will build on.

## Further reading

This guide is built on an essay on Substack:

- Adam Mastroianni, [Science is a strong-link problem](https://substack.com/home/post/p-113948655), *Experimental History*, 2023.

guides.title: Thinking on paper: research notebooks
guides.summary: Published papers hide how research was done. Notebooks keep it. From Newton's Waste Book to Faraday's numbered diaries, the great experimenters thought on paper. Here is what they did, and a simple notebook practice for your own research.
guides.body:
A published paper is not a record of how its results were found. Dead ends, wrong guesses and false starts disappear, and a clean argument remains. The record of how research is actually done lives elsewhere, in notebooks. Their history shows that the best researchers used them not only as memory, but as a tool for thinking.

## A short history

- **Commonplace books.** In the Renaissance, scholars copied quotations and facts into personal notebooks organised by theme. Natural philosophers such as Robert Boyle and Robert Hooke adapted the habit to record their own observations.
- **Newton's Waste Book.** Newton took over an unfinished notebook of his stepfather and filled it with mathematics and physics. Bookkeepers called a "waste book" the place for rough notes, later copied neatly into a ledger. Newton returned to it for years, and it fed his later work.
- **Starkey's tags.** The seventeenth-century chemist George Starkey marked each step of his experiments with labels such as *conjectural process*, *probable conclusion*, *observation*, *criticism* and *refuted by fire*, that is, rejected by experiment.
- **Faraday's diary.** Michael Faraday kept a laboratory diary for over forty years and numbered its paragraphs, more than sixteen thousand of them. He recorded failures as well as successes and added indexes when it grew too large. His memory was poor, and he still sometimes repeated experiments he had forgotten.
- **Joule's numbers.** James Joule kept terse, numerical notebooks written as he measured, close to the excise books of the brewing trade he came from.

Two styles appear: the narrative notebook, which tells what happened and what it means, and the numerical notebook, which records data as it comes. Most researchers need both.

## Why notebooks matter now

- **Memory is unreliable.** Faraday repeated forgotten experiments, and the chemist Joseph Priestley admitted forgetting what he had published. You will forget your failed attempts first.
- **Writing is thinking.** Newton's notebook was an extension of his mind, not an archive. Writing an argument down shows where it breaks.
- **The path matters later.** When a referee asks why you did not try another method, the answer is in your notebook. When you write the thesis, so is the story of how the results came.

## A notebook practice

1. **Keep a waste book and a ledger.** The waste book is fast, messy and dated: calculations, ideas, failed attempts. The ledger, weekly, records in clean form what you now know. In mathematics, the ledger can be a LaTeX file of verified statements and proofs.
2. **Date and number every entry**, as Faraday did. A page you cannot find is a page you do not have.
3. **Tag your claims.** Borrow Starkey's idea and mark each entry: *conjecture*, *example*, *proof idea*, *verified*, *refuted*. Refuted entries stay, with the reason.
4. **Write at the time**, not at the end of the day. Faraday himself advised his students to record results while the work was in front of them.
5. **Index regularly.** A short table of contents per month makes old ideas findable.
6. **Paper or screen, deliberately.** Handwriting is more flexible for diagrams and thinking. Digital notes are searchable and easy to back up. Many researchers think on paper and keep the ledger digital.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every entry in my notebook is dated.
- [ ] I record failed attempts with the reason they failed.
- [ ] My claims are tagged as conjecture, verified or refuted.
- [ ] Once a week, I copy what I now know into a clean ledger.
- [ ] I can find an idea from three months ago in under five minutes.

## Summary

- Papers hide the path of research. Notebooks keep it.
- The great experimenters used notebooks to think, not only to remember.
- Keep a dated waste book for rough work and a clean ledger for what is known.
- Tag claims, keep refutations, write at the time, index regularly.

## Further reading

This guide draws on an essay published on Substack:

- Ulkar Aghayeva, [A Brief History of Lab Notebooks](https://substack.com/home/post/p-192991315), *Asimov Press*, 2026.

For the history in depth, see Frederic L. Holmes, Jürgen Renn and Hans-Jörg Rheinberger (eds.), *Reworking the Bench: Research Notebooks in the History of Science* (2003).

guides.title: Mental health during the PhD
guides.summary: Depression and anxiety are common among doctoral students, and much of the risk comes from how the work is organised. Know the evidence, recognise the warning signs early, protect what helps, and ask for help before things become serious.
guides.body:
A doctorate combines long uncertainty, isolation, high standards, financial pressure and an unclear future. It is not surprising that many doctoral students struggle. It is important to know that this is common, that it is not a personal failure, and that help works best when it comes early. This guide is general information, not medical advice. If you are struggling, talk to a professional.

## What the evidence says

- A study of 3,659 doctoral students in Flanders, Belgium, published in *Research Policy* in 2017, found that about one in two experienced psychological distress and about one in three was at risk of a common psychiatric disorder, especially depression. These rates were higher than in comparable highly educated groups outside academia.
- A systematic review and meta-analysis published in *Scientific Reports* in 2021 pooled studies from several countries. It estimated that about 24% of doctoral students have clinically significant symptoms of depression and about 17% of anxiety, with wide variation between studies.

These numbers are estimates from surveys, and they vary by country, field and method. They show one thing clearly: if you are struggling, you are far from alone.

## What increases the risk

The Belgian study looked at which working conditions go with mental health problems. The strongest links were:

- conflict between work and family or private life,
- high demands combined with little control over one's own work,
- the supervisor's leadership style,
- the decision-making culture of the team,
- a pessimistic view of careers outside academia.

Many of these are features of the environment, not of the person. Some can be changed: how meetings with the supervisor work, how much control you have over your schedule, whether you know that careers outside academia exist and are valued.

## Warning signs

Pay attention when these last for more than two weeks:

- persistent low mood, emptiness or irritability,
- loss of interest in research and in things you used to enjoy,
- sleeping much more or much less than usual,
- constant worry, tension or panic,
- difficulty concentrating, even on simple tasks,
- withdrawing from colleagues, friends and family,
- feeling worthless or that things will not get better.

These signs are a reason to talk to a professional, not a judgment on your ability as a researcher.

## What helps

- **Talk early.** To a friend, another doctoral student, a mentor, your supervisor if you trust them. Saying it aloud often changes how heavy it feels.
- **Use professional help.** Most universities offer free and confidential counselling for students. A general practitioner or family doctor is another starting point. Effective treatments exist.
- **Protect sleep, movement and meals.** They are the base everything else rests on.
- **Keep a life outside research.** Friends, sport, family, a hobby. Your identity is more than your thesis.
- **Reduce isolation.** Work some days in a shared space, join a reading group, go to seminars.
- **Clarify expectations.** Many worries come from not knowing what is expected. The guide [What a PhD expects from you](phd-expectations.html) lists the questions to ask your supervisor.
- **Know your options.** A leave of absence, a change of supervisor or project, or stopping the PhD are legitimate choices. Doctoral schools have contacts for difficulties with supervision.

## If you are in crisis

If you have thoughts of harming yourself, or feel unable to keep yourself safe, contact your local emergency number or a crisis line now. Your university counselling service or doctor can also help you find immediate support. You do not have to wait until things get worse.

## For supervisors and colleagues

Ask how people are doing, and listen to the answer. Make it normal to talk about difficulties. Know where your university's support services are, so that you can point to them.

## Checklist

- [ ] I know where my university's counselling service is and how to contact it.
- [ ] I have at least one person I can talk to honestly about how I am doing.
- [ ] I sleep, move and eat regularly most weeks.
- [ ] I have a life outside research that I protect.
- [ ] I know the warning signs, and I will ask for help if they last more than two weeks.

## Summary

- Depression and anxiety are common among doctoral students.
- Much of the risk comes from working conditions, not from personal weakness.
- Learn the warning signs, and ask for help early.
- Sleep, people and a life outside research are the base.

## Further reading

The figures in this guide come from two research articles:

- Katia Levecque and coauthors, [Work organization and mental health problems in PhD students](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.respol.2017.02.008), *Research Policy* 46 (2017).
- Emily N. Satinsky and coauthors, [Systematic review and meta-analysis of depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation among Ph.D. students](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-93687-7), *Scientific Reports* 11 (2021).

guides.title: Impostor feelings in research
guides.summary: Many researchers feel they are frauds who will soon be found out, despite clear evidence of their competence. The feeling is common, it is not a diagnosis, and it can be managed. Separate feelings from evidence, keep a record of what you have done, and talk about it.
guides.body:
You were admitted to a doctoral programme, your paper was accepted, you were invited to give a talk, and still you feel that everyone else understands more than you, and that sooner or later someone will notice. This experience has a name, and it is very common among researchers.

## What it is

The psychologists Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes described the **impostor phenomenon** in 1978, in high-achieving women who attributed their success to luck or to others' mistakes rather than to their own ability. It has since been found in men and women, at every career stage.

A systematic review published in the *Journal of General Internal Medicine* in 2020 found reported rates between 9% and 82%, depending on how it was measured. The review notes that it is not a recognised psychiatric diagnosis, but that it often comes with anxiety and depression and is linked to burnout and lower job satisfaction.

## Why research makes it worse

- **You work at the edge of what you know.** Feeling ignorant is the normal state of research, but it is easy to read it as personal inadequacy.
- **You compare your inside with others' outside.** You see your own confusion, failed attempts and drafts. You see others' polished talks and published papers.
- **Feedback is rare and mostly negative.** Referee reports list what is wrong. Rejections are frequent. Praise is rare.
- **Success feels unrepeatable.** Each new problem starts from zero, so past results seem to prove nothing about the next one.

## Feelings and evidence

The organisational psychologist Adam Grant offers a useful reframe. When you think others overestimate you, it is more likely that you underestimate yourself. Others have an outside view: they see your record and the progress you cannot see from the inside.

The practical step is to separate two questions:

1. **What do I feel?** That I do not belong, that I was lucky.
2. **What does the evidence say?** Admissions, results, papers, talks, the judgments of people who know the field.

Feelings are real, but they are not evidence. When they disagree, trust the evidence.

## What helps

- **Keep a record of your work.** A file of results, accepted papers, good feedback, problems you solved. Read it when the feeling comes.
- **Talk about it.** Ask senior colleagues whether they have felt it. Most have. Hearing it from someone you admire is the fastest cure.
- **Name the gap precisely.** "I am a fraud" cannot be fixed. "I do not yet understand spectral sequences" can be fixed with a book and two weeks.
- **Collect your best moments.** Grant recommends the Reflected Best Self exercise: ask a few people for stories of when you were at your best, and look for the common thread.
- **Treat confusion as normal.** If you understood everything, you would not be doing research.
- **Get help when it is heavy.** If the feeling comes with persistent low mood or anxiety, see [Mental health during the PhD](mental-health-phd.html).

## Checklist

- [ ] I keep a written record of my results and positive feedback.
- [ ] I have talked with at least one senior researcher about self-doubt.
- [ ] When I feel inadequate, I write down the precise gap and a plan to fill it.
- [ ] I separate what I feel from what the evidence shows.

## Summary

- Impostor feelings are common at every career stage, and they are not a diagnosis.
- Research makes them worse: constant confusion, rare praise, comparison with polished work.
- Separate feelings from evidence, and trust the evidence.
- Keep a record, talk about it, and turn vague doubt into precise gaps.

## Further reading

- Adam Grant, [Rethinking impostor syndrome and unlocking your hidden potential](https://substack.com/home/post/p-138255029), *Granted*, 2023.
- Dena M. Bravata and coauthors, [Prevalence, Predictors, and Treatment of Impostor Syndrome: a Systematic Review](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11606-019-05364-1), *Journal of General Internal Medicine* 35 (2020).

guides.title: Focus, rest and the unconscious work of research
guides.summary: Hard problems are solved in alternation. Concentrated work, then a step back while the mind keeps working, then new insight. Protect deep focus, accept that your time is finite, use breaks deliberately, and sleep on hard problems.
guides.body:
Many mathematicians and scientists describe the same experience: after days of fruitless work on a problem, the solution appears during a walk, in the shower or on waking. This is not magic and not laziness. It is part of how the mind solves hard problems, and you can organise your work around it.

## Poincaré on the bus

In *Science and Method* (1908), Henri Poincaré described working for two weeks on a problem about the functions he later called Fuchsian. He then left for a geological excursion and forgot mathematics. As he stepped onto a bus in Coutances, the key idea came to him, with full certainty. Back home, he checked it at leisure.

Poincaré insisted on two points. The sudden insight came only after long, intense conscious work. And it still had to be verified carefully, because such insights are sometimes wrong.

The psychologist Graham Wallas turned these accounts into four stages of creative thinking in 1926: **preparation**, **incubation**, **illumination** and **verification**.

## What research shows

- **Incubation is real.** A meta-analysis by Sio and Ormerod in *Psychological Bulletin* (2009) found a positive effect of setting a problem aside before returning to it.
- **Preparation comes first.** The effect was larger after longer periods of work on the problem. A break helps only if you have really engaged with it.
- **Light activity can beat total rest.** For some kinds of problems, a break filled with an undemanding task, such as walking or tidying, gave a stronger effect than doing nothing. A break filled with demanding work gave a smaller effect.
- **Sleep consolidates learning.** A large body of research shows that sleep after learning helps memory and the reorganisation of what was learned. Sleeping on a hard problem is good advice.

## Protect deep focus

Incubation only works after real preparation, and real preparation needs uninterrupted attention.

- **Block time for deep work.** Two to four hours without email, messages or meetings, several days a week.
- **Limit switching.** Research by Sophie Leroy (2009) found that when people switch tasks, part of their attention stays on the previous one. She called it attention residue. Finish a session at a clear stopping point before switching.
- **Write down where you are.** At the end of a session, note the open question and the next step. It frees your mind and makes the next start easy.

## Accept that time is finite

The writer Oliver Burkeman argues in *Four Thousand Weeks* (2021) that most productivity advice promises a day when you will finally be on top of everything, and that this day never comes. A life of about four thousand weeks is too short to do everything. Choosing what to neglect is part of doing anything well. For research, this means:

- a small number of active projects at once,
- accepting that some good ideas will never be pursued,
- judging a week by whether the important work moved, not by how many tasks were done.

## A working rhythm

1. **Prepare.** Work on the problem with full attention: examples, attempts, notes.
2. **Step away.** Walk, exercise, do a simple task. Keep the problem loosely in mind, without forcing it.
3. **Sleep on it.** Review the problem briefly in the evening, and write down what comes to mind in the morning.
4. **Return and verify.** Check every insight carefully, as Poincaré did.

Do not mistake avoidance for incubation. A break after hours of real work is incubation. Weeks away from a problem you never really started is not.

## Checklist

- [ ] I have protected blocks of deep work in my week.
- [ ] I end each work session by writing the next step.
- [ ] I take real breaks after intense work, often with light activity.
- [ ] I sleep enough, especially when working on a hard problem.
- [ ] I have a small number of active projects and accept leaving some ideas aside.
- [ ] I verify every sudden insight before trusting it.

## Summary

- Hard problems are solved in alternation: preparation, incubation, illumination, verification.
- Incubation works after real preparation, and light activity or sleep helps.
- Protect deep focus and limit task switching.
- Time is finite: choose few projects and let some ideas go.

## Further reading

- Ut Na Sio and Thomas C. Ormerod, [Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review](https://doi.org/10.1037/a0014212), *Psychological Bulletin* 135 (2009).
- Henri Poincaré, *Science and Method* (1908), chapter on mathematical invention.
- Oliver Burkeman, *Four Thousand Weeks: Time Management for Mortals* (2021). His essay [Life's Short. So Stop Trying to Perfect It.](https://substack.com/home/post/p-150072271) appeared in *The Free Press* on Substack in 2024.
